items.title: Agglutination & the plural
items.subtitle: Building words like Lego bricks
objectifs: Understand the logic of chained suffixes

blocks.text: Turkish is an agglutinative language: instead of separate words (of, to, my, your…), you glue bricks of meaning onto the end of a word. A single Turkish word can be a whole sentence. The classic example:
Four bricks, zero function words. It is exactly the same principle as French « ardoise-s »… but generalised to everything: possession, case, tense, person.
The plural: -ler / -lar
After a number, the noun stays singular: üç elma (three apples), never « üç elmalar ». You can make the quantity explicit with tane: üç tane elma (three apples, literally « three pieces of apple »).
The order of the bricks
Suffixes always arrive in the same order, like a recipe: 1. plural → 2. possessive → 3. case. So evlerimde = ev-ler-im-de. Reversing the order is impossible.
This mechanism moves from the most general to the most specific: the basic object, then quantity, then the possessor, then the role in the sentence.

The genitive (-in) links two nouns: it goes on the possessor, and the possessive goes on the thing possessed. evin kapısı = the door of the house (ev-in + kapı-sı). The genitive closes the first word; it does not slot into the internal order of the second.
When you see a long Turkish word, don't panic: peel it from the right. Look for -ler/-lar (plural), then a suffix you know. The « onion-peeling » reading makes 90% of long words transparent.

lines.name: Magloire
lines.tr: Merhaba! Üç tane elma ve iki ekmek, lütfen.
lines.fr: Hello! Three apples and two loaves of bread, please.

lines.name: Esnaf
lines.tr: Buyurun. Başka bir şey ister misiniz?
lines.fr: Here you go. Would you like anything else?

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: Are the tomatoes good?

lines.name: Esnaf
lines.fr: Very fresh! They arrived this morning.

lines.name: Magloire
lines.tr: O zaman beş tane domates de alın.
lines.fr: Then I'll take five tomatoes as well.

lines.name: Esnaf
lines.fr: That comes to twenty lira in total. Enjoy your meal!

quiz.exp: ev-ler-im-de: house + plural + my + in = in my houses.
ev-im-de: house + my + in. Without the plural, evlerimde would mean « in my houses ».
i (front vowel) → -ler: şehirler.

quiz.q: After a number (e.g. üç elma), the noun is…
quiz.exp: üç elma, beş kitap: the number is enough, no plural after a numeral.

quiz.q: The correct order of suffixes is…
quiz.exp: Always: plural → possessive → case (ev-ler-im-de).
u/o = back vowels → -lar: çocuklar.

items.title: Family & possession
items.subtitle: My, your, his/her: suffixes again
objectifs: Introduce the members of your family
Ask « whose? » and « what is it? »

blocks.text: In French, possession uses separate words (mon, ta, ses…). In Turkish, it uses suffixes attached to the possessed noun, harmonised of course.

If the word ends in a vowel, a buffer n comes in between for the third person: araba (car) → arabası (his/her car), oda → odası (his/her room). For the other persons we use y: arabam… no: araba + -m → arabam (my car, directly), odam. Above all, remember the third-person -sı/-si, which is very frequent.
Introducing your family

items.fr: My mother is a teacher, my father an engineer.
My older sister lives in Izmir.
Who is that? : That's my older sister.

blocks.text: Turkish distinguishes family members precisely: <tur>abla</tur> = older sister, <tur>abi</tur> = older brother, <tur>kız kardeş</tur> = younger sister, <tur>erkek kardeş</tur> = younger brother. And « abla/abi » are also used politely for older strangers!

To say « my mother's first name », you use the genitive: annemin adı (annem-in ad-ı) = literally « my-mother's her-name ». Two suffixes in a row: Turkish possession is reflexive: the possessed noun also carries the mark of its possessor.

lines.name: Elif
lines.fr: Look at this photo! That's my family.

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: Very nice! Who is that?

lines.name: Elif
lines.fr: That's my older sister. Her name is Zeynep.

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: And this one? The child is very cute.

lines.name: Elif
lines.fr: My nephew! My older sister's son.

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: How old is he?

lines.name: Elif
lines.fr: Five. Very naughty!

quiz.exp: anne + -m (1st person) = my mother.
baba + -sı (3rd person) = his/her/their father.
After a vowel, buffer n + -ı/-i: araba-sı.

opts: my nephew on my brother's side
quiz.exp: abla-m-ın (of my older sister) + oğul→oğlu (her son). The possessed noun carries both marks.
yeğen = nephew/niece (the son or daughter of a brother or sister).

items.title: Var / yok: « to have » the Turkish way
items.subtitle: « There is » and « I don't have » without a verb
objectifs: Express possession (I have / I don't have)
Say what there is (or isn't) somewhere

blocks.text: Second big surprise: Turkish has no verb « to have ». You say literally « to me, it exists » or « to me, it does not exist », using two invariable words: var (there is / existing) and yok (there isn't / non-existent).

The structure: possessor (with possessive suffix) + var/yok. The « to me » complement can also appear at the start with the genitive: Benim bir arabam var (as for me, I have a car): the full form, but not obligatory.
« There is » in a place
Same pair, different use: place + var/yok = there is / there isn't. The place goes in the locative (-de/-da), which you will study in depth in module 10.

items.fr: There is a bed in the room.
There is no bread in the kitchen.
I don't have any money in my wallet.
There are two beers in the fridge.

blocks.text: The question: var mı? yok mu?
You add the particle <tur>mi</tur>: <tur>Kahve var mı?</tur> (is there coffee?), <tur>Para yok mu?</tur> (isn't there any money?). The short answer is very simple: <tur>Var.</tur> / <tur>Yok.</tur>

<tur>Yok</tur> is a deeply Turkish word: you hear it all day long. A shopkeeper: « Coca-Cola var mı? » : « Yok, maalesef. » It also expresses total absence and serves as a familiar negative answer (« no, nothing »).

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: Hello, I have a reservation.

lines.name: Resepsiyon
lines.fr: Welcome. Your room is 305. Here is the key.

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: Is there air conditioning in the room?

lines.name: Resepsiyon
lines.fr: Yes, there is. There's Wi-Fi too.

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: And is there a balcony?

lines.name: Resepsiyon
lines.tr: Maalesef balkon yok, ama deniz manzarası var.
lines.fr: Unfortunately no balcony, but there is a sea view.

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: Very good, thank you!

quiz.exp: param (my money) + yok (doesn't exist) = I don't have any money.

quiz.q: How do you ask « is there tea? »
quiz.exp: Çay var mı?: the question particle mi comes directly after var.

quiz.q: « Odada bir yatak var »: where is the bed?
quiz.exp: oda-da = in the room (locative suffix -da).

quiz.q: To say « we have a problem »…
quiz.exp: sorun-umuz (our problem) + var: bir sorunumuz var.

opts: There is beer in the fridge
The fridge is empty of beer
quiz.exp: In the fridge (buzdolabı-nda), beer does not exist: there is no beer in the fridge.

items.title: The present continuous: -iyor
items.subtitle: What you are doing right now

blocks.text: The present tense is called şimdiki zaman (the tense of now). Its central brick: -iyor, inserted between the verb root and the personal ending. Pattern: root + -iyor + person.

Notice the mechanism: yap- (root) + -ıyor (present) + -um (I). The vowel of -iyor harmonises with the root: geliyorum (I am coming), bakıyorum (I am looking), sürüyor… but the endings (-um, -sun, Ø, -uz, -sunuz, -lar) stay stable.
The negative: -miyor
You slip -me/-ma in just before -iyor: yapmıyorum (I am not doing), gelmiyor (he/she is not coming), sevmiyorum (I don't like it). Easy to spot: the little m that crosses out the verb.
Uses

items: Action in progress: <tur>Şimdi ders çalışıyorum.</tur> (I'm studying right now)
Habit: <tur>Her sabah kahve içerim</tur>… in the simple present: but in speech, <tur>Her sabah kahve içiyorum</tur> (I drink coffee every morning) is very common.
Long-lasting states: <tur>İstanbul'da yaşıyorum.</tur> (I live in Istanbul)

blocks.text: Watch the y in -iyor after a vowel: okuyorum (I am reading), bekleyor (he/she is waiting). This y is a real sound, not an ornament.

lines.name: Elif
lines.fr: Hello, Magloire? What are you doing?

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: I'm cooking. And you?

lines.name: Elif
lines.tr: Ben müzik dinliyorum. Yarın sinemaya gidiyoruz, geliyor musun?
lines.fr: I'm listening to music. Tomorrow we're going to the cinema, are you coming?

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: What are you watching (as a film)?

lines.name: Elif
lines.fr: The new Turkish film. It's supposed to be very funny!

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: That works, I'm coming! What time are you meeting?

lines.name: Elif
lines.fr: At seven, in front of the cinema.

quiz.exp: gel (root of to come) + -iyor + -um: I am coming.
bak- contains a (back vowel) → bakıyorum.
The negative -me/-ma slips in between: yap-mı-yorum.

quiz.q: « Ne yapıyorsun? »: what do you answer if you are reading?
quiz.exp: oku (to read) + -yorum: kitap okuyorum = I am reading a book.

quiz.q: How do you say « I live in Istanbul »?
quiz.exp: Two possible verbs: yaşamak or oturmak, with -da (locative): İstanbul'da yaşıyorum / oturuyorum.
